blocks.text: The kinglet, and the bee-eater, and Progne with her red breast know how to zinzilulare [twitter] in a like measure. [III, 55] However that may be, whatever is adduced about the love and gratitude of bee-eaters toward their parents does not meet the point. For in that case רחם racham would not be a φιλότεκνος [philoteknos] bird, as the Hebrews hold, but a φιλοπάτωρ [philopatōr] one. Yet the Hebrew verb רחם racham rather signifies that natural affection and compassion of parents toward their children. And sometimes it is attributed to a father: as in Psal. CIII, 13. כרחם אב על בנים, As a father is merciful toward his children. And Esa. LXIII, 15. 16. Where is the stirring of thy bowels, ורחמיך, and thy mercies, for thou art our father? And Ierem. XXXI, 20. Is not Ephraim a dear son to me? Is he not a delightful child? Therefore my bowels are stirred for him, רחם ארחמנו, I will surely have mercy on him. But maternal affection too is most fittingly expressed by the same verb: as in 1 Reg. III, 26. נכמרו רחמיו, Her (the mother's) affections grew warm toward her son. And Esa. XLIX, 15. Can a woman forget her offspring, מרחם, so as not to have mercy on the son of her womb? And Thren. IV, 10. The hands of the merciful (רחמניות) women (mothers). The Prophet means that the affection of mothers toward their children is natural. Indeed, that affection seems to take its origin from the womb, which in Hebrew is רחם rechem. From these passages it is abundantly clear what the true and native meaning of the verb רחם is, and hence that what the Hebrews assert is true, namely that רחם racham, if the reason for the name is considered, is a φιλότεκνον [philoteknon] bird; although these men, as unskilled in natural history as they were skilled as interpreters of words, were unable to identify that bird.
